name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,307

entries.clue: Notice evidence of measles? (4)

blocks.note: a verb here: to catch sight of
one of the red marks the illness leaves on the skin

annotation.surface: A worried parent looking for signs of a childhood illness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Notice' looks like a noun, a sign on a wall; it is the verb. The question mark flags that one red mark is only a single piece of the evidence.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain verb synonym for catching sight of something, and also the noun for each red blemish of a measles rash.

entries.clue: Manufactured item supporting pipe (7)

blocks.note: a duct is a pipe or channel

annotation.surface: A factory component that holds up a pipe, like a bracket.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supporting pipe' reads as one phrase describing the item; it splits into two pieces instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Whatever a factory turns out and sells is its output, the general word for goods made by industry.

entries.clue: Minor change that’s initially not very effective? (5)

indicatorNotes.initially: at the start, so only the first letter of the word before it counts

annotation.surface: A remark that a small adjustment won't achieve much at first.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the joke: a small adjustment is by nature not very effective, so the wordplay describes the answer too.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal word for a small fine adjustment, as when an engineer adjusts settings slightly.

entries.clue: Briars to upset tree specialist (8)

indicatorNotes.upset: to upset is to knock over and throw into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Thorny bushes annoying the person who looks after the trees.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To' looks like part of the infinitive 'to upset', but its letters are fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: From Latin arbor, 'tree': a professional who prunes, fells and cares for woody plants.

entries.clue: Trouble beginning to affect party (3)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: the beginning of the next word is its first letter

blocks.note: informal British word for a social gathering

annotation.surface: Disruption starting to spoil a celebration.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'do' is British slang for a party, as in 'a birthday do'.
annotation.definitionFit: Means fuss or bother, familiar from the phrases 'much ado about nothing' and 'without further ado'.

entries.clue: Embargoes limiting movement of money? Not at all (2,2,5)

indicatorNotes.limiting: the outer word sets limits all round the inner one
indicatorNotes.movement of: the letters of the next word move out of their order

blocks.note: embargoes are bans; B…ANS goes around the rest

annotation.surface: Sanctions that stop capital flowing across borders.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Movement of money' sounds like finance jargon for capital flows; it is a rearrangement of MONEY sitting inside BANS.
annotation.definitionFit: An emphatic idiom of refusal or denial, as in 'it is by no means certain'.

entries.clue: Come back to minister, one with seat (7)

blocks.note: to seat oneself is to sit

annotation.surface: Returning to see a churchman, one who holds a parliamentary seat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Seat' reads as a noun, a chair or a constituency; it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Literally visiting a place again, and figuratively returning to reconsider an old question or decision.

entries.clue: American aboard vessel cut down oriental food (5)

indicatorNotes.aboard: on board a ship means inside it
indicatorNotes.cut down: shortened, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: SHIP without its final P; S…HI goes around the rest

annotation.surface: A US passenger on a small boat eating an Asian dish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut down' suggests a smaller vessel; it only trims the last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Japanese dish of vinegared rice with raw fish, so an example of East Asian cuisine.

entries.clue: Leaders in Home Office intend to hold line over purchase arrangement (4,4)

indicatorNotes.Leaders in: the leaders of the words that follow are their first letters
indicatorNotes.to hold: the outer word holds the inner letters

blocks.note: first letters of Home and Office
to mean = to intend; ME…AN goes around

annotation.surface: Senior civil servants planning to control a government deal.
annotation.walkthrough: The Home Office is the UK's interior ministry, which makes the clue read like politics rather than mortgages.
annotation.definitionFit: A mortgage: money borrowed from a bank to buy a house, so a financial arrangement behind a purchase.

entries.clue: Former soldier retaining second garment (4)

indicatorNotes.retaining: to retain is to keep hold of, so the outer word keeps the letter inside it

annotation.surface: An ex-serviceman keeping a spare piece of clothing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second' reads as 'spare' or 'another'; it is just the abbreviation S.
annotation.definitionFit: In Britain an undershirt, in North America a waistcoat; either way a specific piece of clothing.

entries.clue: Get rid of boat in Asia (4)

blocks.note: a flat-bottomed Chinese sailing ship with battened sails

annotation.surface: Disposing of a vessel somewhere in Asia.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface runs the two senses together as one act, scrapping a boat; they are two separate meanings of the same word.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal verb for discarding rubbish, and the name of the traditional Chinese sailing vessel.

entries.clue: Feature of St Paul’s criticism, mainly of the family (8)

indicatorNotes.mainly: for the main part, so most of the word, losing its last letter

blocks.note: St Paul's Cathedral in London is famous for its dome

annotation.surface: Commentary on a London cathedral's features, mostly about its family history.
annotation.walkthrough: Stick in the sense of criticism is British informal, as in 'getting stick from the fans'.
annotation.definitionFit: Relating to home and household life, as in domestic chores or a domestic dispute between relatives.

entries.clue: One setting off to read, not fidgeting (9)

indicatorNotes.fidgeting: restless shifting about, so the letters will not keep still in their order

annotation.surface: Someone settling down to read quietly without fidgeting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not fidgeting' reads as sitting still, but 'not' is fodder and 'fidgeting' alone is the indicator; 'setting off' means igniting, not departing.
annotation.definitionFit: The device that triggers an explosive charge, so the thing that sets off a bomb.

entries.clue: Austere saint welcomes joke for the most part (6)

indicatorNotes.welcomes: a host welcomes guests in, so the outer word takes the other inside
indicatorNotes.for the most part: most of the word, losing the last letter

annotation.surface: A severe holy figure who nonetheless enjoys a good joke.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface contrast, a stern saint who likes a laugh, hides that 'welcomes' is only a container signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Both describe severe, unindulgent discipline; a stern regime or rules without leniency.

entries.clue: Top prize money for session of cricket (7)

indicatorNotes.Top: to top a plant is to cut off its head, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: WINNINGS with its first letter removed

annotation.surface: The biggest cash award for a cricket match.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Top prize money' wants to mean the best payout; 'top' is a verb removing the W.
annotation.definitionFit: In cricket, the period when one team or batter takes a turn batting, a basic division of play.

entries.clue: A second pupil, not entirely perceptive (6)

indicatorNotes.not entirely: not the whole word, so the last letter goes

annotation.surface: Describing a runner-up student who is only partly sharp.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not entirely perceptive' reads as a verdict on the pupil; 'not entirely' belongs to the pupil and 'perceptive' stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Shrewd and quick to see how things really are, a near synonym for sharp-witted insight.

entries.clue: Someone scolding in manner carried weight (7)

indicatorNotes.in: the first part is put in the second

blocks.note: tone = manner of speaking; TON…E goes around
a nag is a person who scolds

annotation.surface: A telling-off whose manner of delivery carried real weight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Carried weight' reads as 'was influential'; here it is a noun phrase, the load a ship carries.
annotation.definitionFit: A ship's cargo capacity or the total load it transports, measured in tons.

entries.clue: Pay ranges in shifts (8)

indicatorNotes.shifts: to shift is to move position, so the letters change places

annotation.surface: Wages vary depending on which work shifts you do.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shifts' looks like work shifts, which suits 'pay'; it is the rearrangement signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Money received for work, so a plain noun synonym for wages or salary.

entries.clue: Main star appearing in surreal phantasy (5)

indicatorNotes.appearing in: the answer makes an appearance inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the last two letters of 'surreal' run on into the first three of 'phantasy'

annotation.surface: The lead actor of a dreamlike fantasy film.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Main star' suggests a lead actor; it means the brightest star in a constellation.
annotation.definitionFit: Astronomers label the brightest star of a constellation with the first Greek letter, as in Alpha Centauri.

entries.clue: Book on Dalton’s debut as film spy (4)

indicatorNotes.debut: a first appearance, so the first letter

annotation.surface: A book about Timothy Dalton's first outing as 007.
annotation.walkthrough: Timothy Dalton did play 007, so the answer sits right in the scene.
annotation.definitionFit: Ian Fleming's secret agent 007, hero of the long-running movie franchise.

entries.clue: New baby? Husband and family mostly bowled over (5)

annotation.definitionNote: BIRTH is the arrival of a new baby, not the baby itself; the question mark flags the stretch

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word, losing the last letter

annotation.surface: A family overwhelmed by the arrival of a baby.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bowled over' reads as delighted, which suits the scene; in a down clue it turns H+TRIB upside down.
annotation.definitionFit: The event of a child arriving into the world; the question mark admits it names the delivery rather than the infant.

entries.clue: Present favourable impression of quick trip (4)

blocks.note: what a press officer does to a story, slanting it
a short drive for pleasure, as in 'a ride out in the car'

annotation.surface: A press officer talking up a short journey.
annotation.walkthrough: The PR sense is the modern 'spin doctor' one; the trip sense is the older British 'go for a spin in the car'.
annotation.definitionFit: Political slang for slanting news favourably, and informal for a brief pleasure drive.

entries.clue: Leaves drinker finally imprisoned by magistrate for drinking session (3,5)

indicatorNotes.finally: at the end, so the last letter of the word before it
indicatorNotes.imprisoned by: locked up inside the next word

blocks.note: beak is British slang for a magistrate; B…EAK goes around

annotation.surface: A drunk jailed by a magistrate after a boozing session.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb (departs); it is the noun, tea leaves. The drinking session is a cuppa at work, not a binge.
annotation.definitionFit: A short pause from work to have a cup of something, so a humble kind of drinking session.

entries.clue: Skill in stage role (not lead) (3)

blocks.note: PART (stage role) without its first letter

annotation.surface: Acting ability shown in a supporting part rather than the lead.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not lead' reads as a minor role, which suits the theatre; it means dropping the leading P.
annotation.definitionFit: Older sense of craft or knack, surviving in phrases like 'the art of conversation'.

entries.clue: Various arts with inks revealing ancient script (8)

indicatorNotes.Various: varied, so the letters come in a different order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters; 'with' joins the two words

annotation.surface: Calligraphy techniques used to decipher an old manuscript.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all penmanship, arts and inks, which fits the definition; 'with' only strings the two fodder words together.
annotation.definitionFit: Classical language of India, written in Devanagari, in which the Vedas were composed.

entries.clue: That chap backed the French scoundrel (4)

indicatorNotes.backed: moved backwards, as a car is backed out, so the letters run in reverse

annotation.surface: A man who supported the French turns out to be a villain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backed' reads as 'supported'; it turns LE round.
annotation.definitionFit: Dated slang for a cad or contemptible man, someone who behaves dishonourably.
